units.goal: Count, tell dates, and describe quantities and measurements in Arabic.

lessons.title: Numbers
objectives: Count from one upward in Arabic
Read a simple quantity

tasks.text: Read through this lesson's vocabulary and grammar notes.
Write each new word or form three times by hand.
Use each new word or form in a short sentence of your own.
Cover the vocabulary and try to recall each word from its English gloss.

bookPages.title: Chapter Opener — Talking Numbers
thingsToRemember: Numbers are not a side topic in Arabic — they feed directly into days, months, prices, and weather, so this chapter unlocks a lot of ordinary conversation.
The single biggest thing to hold onto from this page: Arabic script runs right to left, but Arabic numerals run left to right, the same direction as English.
instructions: Read the 'In This Chapter' box first. It's three lines and it tells you exactly what you're accountable for by the end.
Read the opening section straight through without taking notes. You're orienting, not studying.
Slow down at the paragraph explaining number direction. This is the one idea on the page that will save you confusion on every page after it.
Move on as soon as you can state out loud, in your own words, why numbers run the opposite direction from the script.

bookPages.title: Arabic Numerals 0–10 and 11–20
thingsToRemember: Learn 0 through 10 cold before you touch the teens. The teens are built out of them, so time spent here pays twice.
Read each numeral, its pronunciation, and its value as one unit. Learning the shape without the sound leaves you unable to use it in speech.
instructions: Cover the English column and work down the first table, saying each numeral out loud. Uncover to check.
Write the numerals 0 through 10 in your notebook, one line each, until the shapes come without hesitation.
Only then move to the second table. Notice the teens follow a repeating construction rather than being ten new words to memorise.
Play the chapter audio and shadow the pronunciations — say them at the same time as the recording, not after.
Self-check before moving on: have someone call out a number 0 to 20 in English and write the Arabic numeral from memory.

bookPages.title: Numerals 20–100, and the Days of the Week
thingsToRemember: The tens work like the English '-ty' ending — one suffix does the job across the whole range, so this is a pattern to learn once, not nine words to memorise.
The days of the week are derived from the numbers. If you know the numerals, you already have most of the week for free.
Spotting the number root inside a day name is the skill being trained here, not raw memorisation.
instructions: Read the tip about the tens suffix before you look at the table. Going in with the pattern makes the table read as confirmation instead of a list.
Go down the 20–100 table and say each one out loud, listening for the shared ending.
Move to the days section. For each day, find the number hiding inside it and write the pair in your notebook — the day and the number it comes from.
Say the days in order, from memory, twice.
If a day feels arbitrary, you've probably missed its number root. Go back and find it before continuing.

lessons.title: Days, Months & Dates
objectives: Say today's day and roughly when in the month it is
Recognize the words for day and month

tasks.text: Read through this lesson's vocabulary and grammar notes.
Write each new word or form three times by hand.
Use each new word or form in a short sentence of your own.
Cover the vocabulary and try to recall each word from its English gloss.

bookPages.title: The Remaining Days, and the Two Calendars
thingsToRemember: Two of the days break the number pattern — those are the ones that need separate attention, and they carry the cultural weight of the week.
Arabic speakers work with more than one calendar system, so knowing month names in only one of them leaves real gaps.
The Gregorian month names will feel familiar. Read them as a light pass, not a memorisation drill.
instructions: Read the top of the page and note which days are not derived from numbers, and why.
Read the Cultural Wisdom box properly rather than skipping it. It explains the meaning behind a day name, and meaning is what makes vocabulary stick.
Read the explanation of the two calendar systems and be able to state the difference between them in one sentence.
Skim the Gregorian month table — these are close enough to English that you only need recognition, not drilling.
Do not try to memorise both calendars in one sitting. Gregorian today, Islamic on the next page.

bookPages.title: The Islamic Calendar and the Seasons
thingsToRemember: The Islamic months are genuinely new vocabulary — unlike the Gregorian ones, nothing here is guessable from English.
Because the Islamic calendar follows the lunar cycle, its months do not line up with Gregorian months. Trying to map them one-to-one will mislead you.
You already know several of these month names from the religious calendar, so lean on what you have rather than starting from zero.
instructions: Work down the Islamic calendar table slowly, saying each month out loud.
Mark the months you already recognise from religious practice. Those are done — spend your time on the rest.
Write the unfamiliar months in your notebook, grouped in threes. Three at a time is a manageable memorisation chunk; twelve at once is not.
Read the note on why the two calendars drift apart, and make sure you understand that a given Islamic month is not fixed to any Gregorian one.
Finish with the four seasons at the bottom of the page — a short, easy win to close the session on.

lessons.title: Measurements
objectives: Use a basic unit of weight or length in a sentence
Ask how much something weighs or measures

tasks.text: Read through this lesson's vocabulary and grammar notes.
Write each new word or form three times by hand.
Use each new word or form in a short sentence of your own.
Cover the vocabulary and try to recall each word from its English gloss.

bookPages.title: Size Matters — Measuring in Arabic
thingsToRemember: This is a short list of high-frequency, immediately usable words — shopping, cooking, directions, describing anything.
Several units are borrowed from the metric system and will sound close to their English equivalents, so the list is smaller than it first looks.
Measurement words pair naturally with the numbers you just learned. Practising them together is more efficient than practising either alone.
instructions: Read the list once and separate it into two groups: the units that sound close to English and the ones that don't.
The near-English ones need recognition only. Give them one pass.
Write the remaining units in your notebook with a real-world example beside each.
Combine what you know: say several measurements out loud pairing a number from earlier in the chapter with a unit from this page.
Test yourself by describing three objects near you using a number plus a unit.

bookPages.title: Fun & Games — Name the Four Seasons
thingsToRemember: Write answers in your notebook, not in the book, so you can retake this later.
This checks recall of the seasons from page 75. If it feels hard, the gap is on that page, not this one.
instructions: Label your notebook A through D to match the four illustrations.
Work out each season from the picture and write it in Arabic. Attempt all four before checking anything.
Resist flipping back to page 75 mid-exercise — testing yourself is what moves the vocabulary into memory, and looking it up skips that.
Check your answers against Appendix C at the back of the book.
Anything you missed, return to page 75, redrill just that season, and retake the exercise tomorrow.
Bar for finishing Chapter 5: you can count 0 to 100, name the days and both sets of months, and use a handful of measurement units in a sentence.

units.title: At the Office and Around the House
units.goal: Name common objects and describe everyday activities at the office and at home.

lessons.title: At the Office
objectives: Name common objects found at an office
Describe what you do at work

tasks.text: Read through this lesson's vocabulary and example phrases.
Say each new word or phrase out loud a few times.
Describe something using at least two of today's new words.
Quiz yourself on today's vocabulary from memory.

bookPages.title: Chapter Opener — Managing the Office Environment
instructions: Read the 'In This Chapter' box first — three bullets telling you what you're accountable for.
Read the opening section straight through. You're orienting, not memorizing.
Note the two anchor words for house and office. Nearly everything in this chapter hangs off one or the other.
Read the Cultural Wisdom box properly. The workweek in most Arabic-speaking countries runs on different days than you're used to, and that detail shows up in conversation constantly.
Move on once you can say which two settings this chapter covers and name each in Arabic.

bookPages.title: Office Vocabulary
instructions: Work down the list saying each item out loud with its pronunciation.
Mark the items that are physically near you right now. Those are the ones you'll actually retain, so drill them first.
Write the rest in your notebook grouped by where they live — desk, room, building.
Point at real objects around you and name them in Arabic. Anything you can't name, circle in your notebook.
Come back to the circled ones tomorrow rather than grinding them now.

bookPages.title: Interacting with Your Colleagues
instructions: Read the intro paragraph before touching the lists — it frames why role vocabulary matters more in Arabic workplaces than you'd expect.
Notice that most role words come in masculine and feminine pairs. Learn both together; learning one and guessing the other will get you wrong endings.
Write out the pairs side by side in your notebook so the pattern between them is visible on the page.
Pick the five roles that describe people you actually deal with and say a sentence about each out loud.
Self-check: cover the Arabic and produce both gender forms from the English.

bookPages.title: Workplace Phrases and Talkin' the Talk
instructions: Finish the phrase list from the previous page, reading each aloud.
Move to the Talkin' the Talk dialogue. Read it once silently for the gist — don't stop at unknown words.
Read it a second time out loud, taking both parts.
On the third pass, underline any phrase you'd actually use at work. Those are worth memorizing; the rest is context.
Dialogues are where isolated vocabulary turns into usable speech, so don't skip past them to get to the next list.

bookPages.title: Talkin' the Talk — Conference Report Dialogue
instructions: Read the whole exchange through once without looking anything up.
Read it again out loud, switching between the speakers so you hear both sides.
Find the question forms — asking whether something is ready or finished is the most reusable pattern on this page.
Cover the English and work through the Arabic alone. Check only where you stall.
Try replacing the subject of the conversation with something from your own work and say the exchange again.

bookPages.title: Words to Know — Office Terms
instructions: This box collects the chapter's office vocabulary in one place. Treat it as your checkpoint, not new material.
Cover the English column and work down the list. Mark anything you can't produce.
Copy only the marked items into your notebook. Copying words you already know wastes the session.
Note the masculine and feminine markers — several entries change form depending on who you're describing.
Repeat the cover-and-test until you can clear the full list twice in a row.

bookPages.title: Giving Orders — The Imperative
instructions: This is the grammar core of the chapter. Slow down — the vocabulary pages were warm-up.
Read the explanation of how the imperative is built from the regular verb before looking at any table.
The key idea: commands are derived from a form you already know, not learned separately. Make sure that's clear before continuing.
Write out the derivation for two or three verbs in your notebook, showing the regular form and the command form side by side.
Say each command out loud. Imperatives are spoken forms — reading them silently doesn't build the reflex.

bookPages.title: Imperative Tables and Supplying Your Office
instructions: Work through the imperative tables one pronoun at a time. Look across the row: pronoun, regular form, command form.
The pattern repeats across verbs. Once you see it in the first table, the second should confirm rather than surprise you.
Copy one full table into your notebook by hand. Copying a conjugation table is one of the few times rote writing genuinely helps.
Move to the office supplies list and read each item aloud.
Combine the two halves of the page: give yourself commands about supplies out loud. That pairing is the point of putting them together.

bookPages.title: Computer and Equipment Terms
instructions: Read the equipment list, noting how many terms are borrowed from English and just adapted to Arabic sounds.
Those borrowed ones need recognition only. Give them one pass and spend your time on the native terms.
Study the pronoun table at the bottom carefully — this is the scaffolding for talking about who owns or uses what.
Write five sentences in your notebook pairing a pronoun with a piece of equipment.
Say each sentence out loud before moving on.

bookPages.title: Pronoun Forms and Talkin' the Talk
instructions: Finish the pronoun table, reading each row across so the pronoun and its form stay linked.
Move into the dialogue. First pass silently for gist.
Second pass out loud, taking both speakers.
Find the pronouns in the dialogue and connect each back to the table you just read. Seeing them used is what makes the table stick.
Note how the exchange opens and closes — greetings and sign-offs transfer to almost any workplace conversation.

bookPages.title: Words to Know, and Life at Home
instructions: Finish the dialogue at the top of the page.
Work the Words to Know box — it's short. Note that the apology form changes depending on whether a man or a woman is speaking.
Say both forms out loud and use the one that applies to you until it's automatic.
The Life at Home section starts the chapter's second half. Read the intro and mentally switch settings from office to house.
Good stopping point if you're running low on focus. The home vocabulary deserves a fresh session.

lessons.title: Around the House
objectives: Name the rooms of a house
Describe where something is in the house

tasks.text: Read through this lesson's vocabulary and example phrases.
Say each new word or phrase out loud a few times.
Describe something using at least two of today's new words.
Quiz yourself on today's vocabulary from memory.

bookPages.title: Rooms of the House
instructions: Read the room list aloud, then walk through your actual home naming each room in Arabic as you enter it.
That physical walkthrough does more for retention than three passes at the list.
Note the words for items that live in specific rooms — they're grouped that way on purpose.
Write each room in your notebook with two things that belong in it.
Self-check: name every room in your home in Arabic without looking.

bookPages.title: Family Life in a Middle Eastern Home
instructions: Read the cultural section properly rather than skimming to the dialogue. It explains household norms that make the vocabulary make sense.
Note which family relationships get their own specific word where English uses a general one. Those distinctions matter and have no English shortcut.
Read the Talkin' the Talk dialogue once silently, then once out loud taking every part.
Map each speaker to their family role as you read.
Try describing your own household using the vocabulary from this page.

bookPages.title: Talkin' the Talk — Around the House
instructions: Read the exchange through once for gist.
Read it again out loud taking every speaker.
Find the question about where something is. That pattern is one of the highest-value structures in the whole chapter — you'll use it daily.
Notice the imperatives appearing naturally in the household requests. That's the grammar from page 85 showing up in real speech.
Cover the English and work the Arabic alone before moving on.

bookPages.title: Words to Know — Household Terms
instructions: Second checkpoint box of the chapter — this one covers the home half.
Cover the English and work down the list. Mark what you can't produce.
Copy only the marked items into your notebook.
Then do the reverse: cover the Arabic and produce it from the English. That direction is harder and is what the exercise on the next page will test.
Clear the list twice in a row before attempting Fun & Games.

bookPages.title: Fun & Games — Label the Household Scene
instructions: Write answers in your notebook, not in the book, so you can retake this later.
Work from the illustration to the word, not the other way round. That direction is what recall actually looks like.
Attempt every item before checking anything. Guess rather than skip — a wrong guess you then correct sticks better than a blank.
Check against Appendix C at the back of the book.
Anything you missed, go back to the Words to Know box on page 93, redrill just those items, and retake this tomorrow.
Bar for finishing Chapter 6: you can name the rooms of a house, the main office objects, and form a command from a regular verb without looking it up.
